ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The sides of $\triangle ABC$ have lengths $6, 8$ and $10$. A circle with center $P$ and radius $1$ rolls around the inside of $\triangle ABC$, always remaining tangent to at least one side of the triangle. When $P$ first returns to its original position, through what distance has $P$ traveled?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figures show triangle ABC as a 6-8-10 right triangle, with AB horizontal length 8, BC vertical length 6, and AC length 10. A unit circle with center P is inside the triangle, initially tangent to AB, and an arrow indicates it rolls around inside. Reasoning: Since the circle has radius 1, whenever it is tangent to a side, P is 1 unit from that side. As the circle rolls all the way around the inside and P returns to its starting point, P traces the boundary formed by shifting each side of ABC inward by 1 unit. For the original 6-8-10 right triangle, the area is 6*8/2 = 24 and the semiperimeter is (6+8+10)/2 = 12, so its inradius is 24/12 = 2. The inward-shifted triangle has sides parallel to the original and inradius 2-1 = 1, so it is similar to ABC with scale factor 1/2. Therefore the distance traveled by P is the perimeter of this smaller triangle: (6+8+10)*1/2 = 12.

From the image, note the triangle is the 6-8-10 right triangle and the unit circle is inside tangent to a side, so the center P must stay 1 unit from any side it touches. From the text, read that the circle radius is 1 and that P travels until it returns to its starting position while rolling around the inside. The path of P is the boundary of the triangle formed by shifting each side of ABC inward by 1 unit. Compute the inradius of the original 6-8-10 triangle: area = 6*8/2 = 24 and semiperimeter = 12, so inradius = 24/12 = 2. The shifted triangle has the same angles and inradius 2 - 1 = 1, so it is similar to the original triangle with scale factor 1/2. Therefore its perimeter, which is the distance traveled by P, is (6+8+10)/2 = 12.
